title: Tamil Nadu-Born Non-Binary Academic Wins Seat in Holyrood
excerpt: Q Manivannan becomes one of Scotland's first transgender MSPs — without British citizenship or permanent residency.
body:
Q Manivannan, a Tamil Nadu-born anthropologist and doctoral researcher, made history on May 9, 2026, becoming one of the first openly transgender people elected to the Scottish Parliament — while holding neither British citizenship nor permanent UK residency.

**What happened — a breakthrough at Holyrood:**
Manivannan won a seat on the Edinburgh and Lothians East regional list for the pro-independence Scottish Greens in the 2026 Holyrood election. The election was made possible by a rule change that, as Daily Excelsior reported, 'allowed foreigners on even short-term visas and without indefinite leave to remain to be eligible for elections in Scotland.' As a Commonwealth citizen on a valid visa, Manivannan met the legal threshold to stand.

**Context — a journey from Tamil Nadu to Holyrood:**
Manivannan studied liberal arts at O.P. Jindal Global University in Delhi, then completed an MPhil in international peace studies at Trinity College Dublin, before arriving in Scotland in 2021 for a doctorate in international relations at the University of St Andrews. On the campaign trail, they focused on the cost-of-living crisis, climate change, immigrant rights, and disability inclusion — positioning themself, in their own words, as 'a queer Tamil immigrant' bringing 'a politics of care and compassion to Holyrood.' The Scottish Greens took seven seats in total, a record result for the party.

**What to watch — the visa question:**
Manivannan's current visa is time-limited, meaning they must secure updated immigration status to serve out their full parliamentary term — a situation the Scottish Greens say underscores exactly why UK visa rules need reform.
nri_angle: For Indian-Americans navigating their own hyphenated identity in a Western democracy, Manivannan's election is a vivid reminder that South Asian immigrants are reshaping not just the economy but the very legislatures of the English-speaking world.
author: Diaspora Desk
